title: “CALL THOSE THINGS INTO EXISTENCE” — DID GOD REALLY GIVE CHRISTIANS CREATIVE POWER THROUGH THEIR WORDS?
paragraphs:
“CALL THOSE THINGS INTO EXISTENCE” — DID GOD REALLY GIVE CHRISTIANS CREATIVE POWER THROUGH THEIR WORDS?
Millions of Christians have been told to “speak it into existence.” But what if the verse behind that teaching was never describing your power at all—and what if what Scripture actually promises is far more beautiful?
Maybe you have done it.
You stood in front of a mirror and declared that the sickness was gone.
You spoke prosperity over an empty bank account.
You declared that the relationship would return.
You announced that the job was already yours.
You refused to say anything “negative” because someone warned you that your words might create the very thing you feared.
And somewhere underneath all those declarations was a sentence you had heard preached with breathtaking confidence:
“Call those things which be not as though they were.”
It sounded biblical.
It sounded powerful.
It sounded almost impossible to question because, after all, those words really are connected to Romans 4:17.
But there is a question every follower of Jesus eventually has to be brave enough to ask:
Did God actually give Christians the ability to create reality with their words?
Or have we quietly taken something Scripture says about God…and made it about us?
That question matters more than it first appears.
Because when theology is slightly wrong in comfortable seasons, it can become devastating theology in seasons of suffering.
Imagine the mother praying beside a hospital bed who has been told that acknowledging the seriousness of her child's condition demonstrates unbelief.
Imagine the Christian whose business collapses despite months of declarations.
Imagine the woman desperately praying for a marriage while being told she simply has to “speak” restoration.
Imagine someone grieving a death while secretly wondering whether they failed because their faith was not strong enough.
That is where this teaching stops being merely theoretical.
It enters hospital rooms.
Funerals.
Divorce courts.
Empty bedrooms.
Unemployment lines.
And terrified midnight prayers.
So we need to open the Bible carefully.
Not to destroy faith.
To rescue faith from something God never asked it to carry.
Romans 4:17 contains the famous language. In the Greek text we read:
“θεοῦ τοῦ ζωοποιοῦντος τοὺς νεκροὺς καὶ καλοῦντος τὰ μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα”
The crucial words are:
“καλοῦντος τὰ μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα”
kalountos ta mē onta hōs onta.
The idea is of calling the things that are not as though they are—or, as some translations express the thought, calling into being that which does not exist.
But slow down.
Because one grammatical observation changes the entire conversation.
Who is doing the calling?
Read the words immediately before the famous phrase:
“θεοῦ τοῦ ζωοποιοῦντος…”
theou tou zōopoiountos…
God—the One giving life.
Paul is describing God.
Romans 4:17 is not primarily a command telling Abraham how to speak.
It is a revelation describing the God Abraham believed.
That difference is enormous.

Abraham's faith was extraordinary not because Abraham discovered a divine mechanism for manufacturing reality with vocabulary, but because Abraham trusted the God whose power was greater than Abraham's impossibility.
Paul's focus is not the creative sovereignty of Abraham's mouth.
It is the sovereign power of Abraham's God.
The same God introduced in the opening chapter of Scripture.
“וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים יְהִי אוֹר וַיְהִי־אוֹר”
Vayomer Elohim, yehi or; vayehi or.
“And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.”
Notice who speaks creation into existence.
God.
Genesis does not introduce humanity as independent creators whose sentences possess God's sovereign power. It introduces the LORD as Creator and humanity as His creation.
That distinction does not diminish human dignity.
It establishes it correctly.
We bear God's image.
We are not God.
And sometimes one of the most spiritually dangerous things we can do is take something glorious about God and subtly relocate it into ourselves.
It happened in Eden.
The temptation was not merely about fruit.
It was about the ancient desire to cross the Creator-creature boundary.
“You will be like God.”
Humanity has been reaching for that sentence ever since.
Sometimes through pride.
Sometimes through religion.
And sometimes through Christian vocabulary.
That does not mean your words are powerless.
Far from it.
Scripture treats human speech with frightening seriousness.
Proverbs 18:21 says that death and life are in the power of the tongue and that those who love it will eat its fruit. The Hebrew expression includes:
“מָוֶת וְחַיִּים בְּיַד־לָשׁוֹן”
Maveth vechayyim beyad-lashon.
Death and life are “in the hand”—that is, within the power or agency—of the tongue.
Words can destroy reputations.
Words can fracture marriages.
Words can crush children.
Words can spread lies.
Words can ignite hatred.
Words can manipulate.
Words can also confess truth.
Comfort the grieving.
Defend the vulnerable.
Proclaim Christ.
Ask forgiveness.
Restore relationships.
Bless rather than curse.
Speak courage into someone who has almost surrendered.
Tell a sinner that there really is mercy at the cross.
Words matter enormously.
But “words have consequences” is not the same statement as “human words possess God's sovereign creative power.”
That distinction protects us from turning biblical faith into a Christianized version of manifestation.
The Gospel is not “believe strongly enough in your desired future and your words will attract it.”
The Gospel is not “the universe responds to your frequency.”
The Gospel is not “your mouth creates your reality.”
Christianity begins somewhere completely different.
God is God.
We are sinners.
Christ is Lord.
We cannot save ourselves.
And our hope rests not in mastering spiritual laws but in being reconciled to the Father through Jesus Christ.
Even Mark 11, another passage frequently brought into this discussion, begins with words we dare not rush past.
“Ἔχετε πίστιν θεοῦ.”
Echete pistin theou.
“Have faith in God.”
Then Jesus speaks about commanding a mountain and believing in prayer.
But notice where Jesus places the faith.
Not in faith itself.
Not in verbal technique.
Not in personal creative energy.
In God.
Jesus directs His disciples away from self-reliance and toward the Father.
And the wider biblical teaching about prayer refuses to turn God into a machine controlled by the correct confession.
First John 5:14 says that our confidence is that when we ask according to His will, He hears us.
That phrase matters:
“according to His will.”
Christian prayer is bold.
Christian prayer can be audacious.
Christian prayer expects miracles because our God can do what we cannot.
We can pray for healing.
We can pray for provision.
We can pray for reconciliation.
We can ask God to open doors no human being can open.
We can plead for prodigals to come home.
We can pray against circumstances that look utterly impossible.
But prayer is not the throne commanding the King.
Prayer is the child approaching the Father.
There is authority in Christ.
There is confidence before God.
There is genuine power in prayer.
There are gifts of the Holy Spirit.
There is supernatural intervention.
There is nothing weak about biblical Christianity.
But biblical authority is delegated authority.
We never become sovereign.
Jesus remains Lord.
That becomes painfully important when God's answer is not the answer we wanted.
Jesus Himself shows us what faithful prayer looks like when suffering is approaching.
Gethsemane.
Darkness.
Agony.
The cross drawing closer.
Jesus does not pretend suffering is pleasant.
He does not rename agony as comfort.
He does not teach us that acknowledging pain creates pain.
He pours out His heart before the Father.
And then comes surrender:
“Not my will, but Yours, be done.”
That is not weak faith.
That is perfect faith.
Maybe this is where someone reading these words needs to be released from a burden you have carried for years.
Maybe somebody convinced you that your tragedy happened because you “spoke negatively.”
Maybe you have replayed your sentences trying to discover which words supposedly opened the door.
Maybe someone became sick and you blamed yourself.
Maybe you prayed for healing and healing did not come in the way you begged for it.
Maybe your marriage ended.
Maybe the pregnancy was lost.
Maybe the business failed.
Maybe the person died.
And somewhere in your grief came another wound:
Was my faith too weak?
Listen carefully.
Biblical faith is not pretending the grave is empty when the body is still inside it.
Biblical faith can stand outside Lazarus's tomb and weep.
Jesus did.
Faith can tell the truth about pain without surrendering hope in God.
Abraham himself is the example in Romans 4.
Paul does not portray him as a man refusing to acknowledge reality. Abraham knew the condition of his body. He knew Sarah's barrenness. The impossibility was real.
But the impossibility was not sovereign.
God was.
That is faith.
Not denying reality.
Trusting God beyond reality.
There is a world of difference.
You do not have to call cancer “health” to believe God can heal.
You can say, “This diagnosis is terrifying, but my God is still God.”
You do not have to call poverty “wealth.”
You can say, “I don't know where the provision will come from, but Father, give me this day my daily bread.”
You do not have to pretend your marriage is healthy when it is breaking.
You can tell the truth, seek help, repent where necessary, establish wise boundaries where necessary, and beg Christ for restoration.
You do not have to say, “I am not hurting.”
You can say, “Jesus, I am hurting so badly that I barely know how to pray.”
That is not unbelief.
Sometimes that is the most honest faith you have left.
The Psalms are filled with believers crying, questioning, grieving, remembering, pleading and hoping.
God never required His children to lie about their wounds in order to prove they trusted Him.
And that brings us to something even deeper.
Perhaps the greatest miracle Christianity offers is not that you can speak whatever future you desire into existence.
It is that God can take a future you destroyed and write redemption into it.
That is the heartbeat of grace.
Peter could not unsay his denial.
Three times.
“I don't know Him.”
Words.
Terrible words.
Words spoken by a man who had promised Jesus he would never abandon Him.
Peter's tongue produced something devastating.
But Peter's failure did not get the final sentence.
Jesus met him again.
Grace walked onto the shore.
A charcoal fire burned.
And the disciple who had denied Christ was restored by Christ.
That is our story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal was public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you preached one thing and lived another.
Maybe you have been carrying pornography behind a Christian smile.
Maybe bitterness has been eating you alive.
Maybe pride made you cruel.
Maybe you have manipulated people.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe you walked away from God and still know exactly how to look spiritual when people are watching.
Maybe your mouth has worshiped Jesus on Sunday and destroyed people by Monday.
Then perhaps the question you most desperately need answered is not:
“How can I speak my dream into existence?”
Perhaps it is:
“Can Jesus still redeem someone like me?”
Yes.
Not because your words possess creative sovereignty.
Because His grace is greater than your sin.
You cannot declare yourself righteous.
Christ justifies the ungodly who trust Him.
You cannot speak away your guilt.
Christ carried guilt to the cross.
You cannot manifest resurrection.
Jesus walked out of the tomb.
You cannot create a new heart by positive confession.
God saves.
God forgives.
God regenerates.
God restores.
God transforms.
And suddenly Romans 4:17 becomes far more beautiful than a formula for getting things.
The God “who gives life to the dead” is the center of the sentence.
That is the God Abraham trusted.
And that is the God sinners desperately need.
Because spiritually, our problem was never merely that we lacked enough positive declarations.
We needed resurrection.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed a Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your vocabulary.
He came to save you.
He lived the righteousness you failed to live.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Him finds something no motivational confession could manufacture:
grace.
Real grace.
Grace for the ashamed.
Grace for the addict.
Grace for the hypocrite finally tired of pretending.
Grace for the religious person discovering that religion cannot save.
Grace for the person whose life looks nothing like the testimony they wish they had.
Grace for scandals.
Grace for ruins.
Grace for people who have finally reached the end of themselves.
But grace does not leave us unchanged.
Jesus does not simply rewrite our ending while permitting us to remain in love with the sin destroying us.
Grace calls us to repentance.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace brings hidden things into light.
Grace transforms our speech because grace transforms our hearts.
So should Christians speak differently?
Absolutely.
Speak truth.
Speak Scripture.
Speak encouragement.
Speak blessing rather than cursing.
Confess Christ.
Confess sin.
Pray boldly.
Ask courageously.
Refuse gossip.
Reject slander.
Stop rehearsing hopelessness as though God were absent.
Tell your soul what is true about God.
Tell frightened believers that Christ has not abandoned them.
Tell sinners there is forgiveness.
Tell the brokenhearted there is a Savior.
Tell the world that the tomb is empty.
But never confuse declaring God's truth with possessing God's sovereignty.
Your confidence is not:
“My words control tomorrow.”
Your confidence is:
“My Father already holds tomorrow.”
That is stronger.
Because if your hope rests on the perfection of your confession, then eventually you will become terrified of your own mouth.
But if your hope rests in Jesus Christ, you can pray through tears.
You can stumble over sentences.
You can whisper, “Lord, I believe; help my unbelief.”
You can come empty-handed.
You can admit that you do not understand.
You can tell God exactly how frightened you are.
And you can still be held.
Maybe that is the word somebody desperately needs tonight.
You do not need magical words.
You need Christ.
You do not need to become your own creator.
You need to trust your Creator.
You do not need enough spiritual power to control every chapter.
You need the Savior who already knows how the story ends.
And if this exposed something you have believed, don't hide from the conviction.
Bring it to Scripture.
Bring it to Jesus.
Someone scrolling beneath you may desperately need to discover that they are not the only unfinished person following a perfect Savior.
Let them see the difference.
We want this community to remain a place for Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, repentance, grace and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Come to Jesus.
Not to a formula.
Not to manifestation.
Not to the illusion that you can control the universe if only you learn the correct words.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive grace.
Trust the Father.
Pray boldly.
Speak truth.
Love people.
And when circumstances refuse to obey your voice, remember that they have never escaped His authority.
You were never asked to become God.
You were invited to become His child.
And perhaps that is the sentence worth carrying into every impossible room you will ever enter:
You don't have to speak your future into existence when your future is already in the hands of the God who gives life to the dead.
